input.reason: I read src/ci.ts, where line 4 is `const res = await fetch(`${CI}/builds/${id}`);`. The call has no options object, so it passes no `signal` and sets no timeout. Line 5 then awaits `res.json()`, also with no deadline. I searched src/ for timeout, abort, AbortSignal, Promise.race, undici and global dispatcher configuration and found none. package.json only defines build and test scripts, so nothing sets a timeout globally. The only caller is the `build` route in src/routes.ts:51-53, which awaits `getBuild(req.params.id)` directly with no deadline of its own. `buildRoutes` is not used anywhere else in src/, so nothing wraps the handler with a timeout. No tests exist. The finding holds as written.

findings.text: The CI build request has no timeout or abort signal, so a stalled CI response hangs every caller of `getBuild`.
findings.reason: Claim 1, no timeout or abort signal: src/ci.ts:4 calls `fetch(`${CI}/builds/${id}`)` with no options object, so it passes no `signal`. Line 5 awaits `res.json()` with no deadline either. Nothing in src/ or package.json sets a timeout or dispatcher globally. Claim 2, a stalled CI response hangs every caller: the only caller is the `build` handler at src/routes.ts:52, `return { status: 200, body: await getBuild(req.params.id) };`. It awaits the result directly, and no Promise.race, timeout or other wrapper around the route exists anywhere in src/. A stalled upstream therefore leaves that request waiting.

input.severity_reason: This is a reliability risk that only shows up when the CI service is slow or unresponsive. In that case every `build` route request (src/routes.ts:52) stays open with no deadline set in the code. That can tie up server resources, but it does not affect the normal path when CI responds.
